links.outcome: Physician diagnostic accuracy after exposure to erroneous versus error-free LLM recommendations (automation bias)
links.effect: Mean accuracy 84.9% (error-free) vs 73.3% (flawed); adjusted difference -14.0 percentage points (95% CI -8.3 to -19.7; P<.0001). Top-choice accuracy difference -18.3 points.
links.quote: This trial demonstrates that erroneous LLM recommendations significantly degrade physicians’ diagnostic performance by inducing automation bias, even in AI-trained physicians.

links.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of AI-literacy-trained physicians when exposed to flawed LLM advice
links.effect: Despite 20-hour AI-literacy training, physicians receiving flawed recommendations scored 73.3% vs 84.9% with error-free advice (adjusted difference -14.0 points, P<.0001).
links.quote: This trial demonstrates that erroneous LLM recommendations significantly degrade physicians’ diagnostic performance by inducing automation bias, even in AI-trained physicians.

links.outcome: Physicians' failure to verify erroneous LLM outputs, degrading diagnostic reasoning
links.effect: Flawed LLM recommendations reduced diagnostic reasoning accuracy from 84.9% to 73.3% and top-choice accuracy from 90.5% to 76.1%.
links.quote: Voluntary deference to flawed AI output highlights critical patient safety risk, necessitating robust safeguards to ensure human oversight before widespread clinical deployment.

screen.reason: This is a randomized trial using clinical vignettes to evaluate automation bias when physicians interact with correct vs. deliberately flawed LLM outputs; it does not evaluate a specific safeguard or deployment practice.
